about: Design and Manufacture 1 (MECH40007) is a core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Mechanical Engineering. It introduces the practical side of mechanical design and manufacture: the design process from a customer brief through conceptual and detail design, sketching, CAD and engineering drawing, and workshop manufacturing skills, with students making their own designs in the department's workshops. We could not load the department's full descriptor, so the topic headings here are not taken from a confirmed official topic list; they are a working list cross-checked against the module's aims (a third-party UCEAP copy of the descriptor, last reviewed 2021–22) and a 2023 conference paper on Imperial's design teaching. Check the current descriptor for the exact syllabus and assessment, which we have not stated.

notes.body:
Engineers sketch to think and to communicate. A quick freehand sketch lets you test an idea in seconds, explain it to a teammate or note a measurement in the workshop. A formal drawing, by contrast, defines a part precisely enough for someone else to make it.

Freehand sketching technique
- Start with light construction lines. "Crate" the object in a box of its overall size, then carve features out of it.
- Draw circles in a square (or ellipses in a parallelogram) using guide marks on the centre lines.
- Use darker, heavier lines for the final outline so the important edges stand out.
- Keep proportions right rather than exact dimensions; add key dimensions as annotations.

Pictorial views
- Isometric: the three axes are drawn 120° apart, with the receding axes at 30° to the horizontal. In an isometric drawing, lengths along the axes are drawn full size. (A true isometric projection foreshortens them to about 0.82, but drawings usually ignore this.)
- Oblique: the front face is drawn true shape and the depth axis is drawn at an angle, often 45°. In cabinet oblique the depth is halved so the object does not look stretched.
- Perspective: lines converge to vanishing points. It looks realistic but is harder to measure from.

Orthographic projection
Orthographic views show the object looking straight at each face, one view per direction, so true lengths and shapes can be measured.
- First-angle projection (common in the UK and Europe): imagine the object between you and the drawing plane. The plan (view from above) is placed below the front view, and the view from the left is placed on the right of the front view.
- Third-angle projection (standard in North America): the plane is between you and the object. The plan goes above the front view, and the view from the left goes on the left.
- BS 8888 allows either method, but the drawing must show the projection symbol: a truncated cone shown as a side view and an end view. Read the symbol as a tiny drawing rather than memorising left/right: in first angle the end view (two circles) is drawn on the opposite side from the end of the cone it looks at; in third angle it is drawn on the same side. Check the version in your course notes.

Line types (BS 8888, which applies ISO 128)
- Continuous wide line: visible outlines and edges.
- Continuous narrow line: dimension lines, projection lines, leader lines, hatching.
- Dashed narrow line: hidden edges.
- Long-dash dotted narrow line: centre lines and axes of symmetry.
- Long-dash dotted line, wide at the ends and at changes of direction: cutting planes for sections.

Sections
A section view imagines the part cut along a plane, so internal features can be shown with solid lines instead of confusing hidden lines.
- The cut faces are hatched with narrow lines, usually at 45°.
- By convention, shafts, bolts, pins, keys and thin ribs cut along their length are not hatched.

Scales
The preferred scales (BS EN ISO 5455) include 1:1, 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 2:1, 5:1 and 10:1. The scale goes in the title block, but dimensions always show the real size.

Exam tips: check which projection a drawing uses before reading it. Hidden detail and centre lines are among the most commonly forgotten features.

Parametric solid modelling (in packages such as SolidWorks, Fusion or Creo) builds a 3D part as a sequence of features, each driven by dimensions and constraints. Changing a dimension later updates the whole model, provided it was built sensibly.

Sketches and constraints
Most features start from a 2D sketch on a plane or a flat face. A sketch is controlled in two ways:
- Geometric constraints, or relations: horizontal, vertical, coincident, tangent, parallel, perpendicular, equal, concentric, symmetric.
- Dimensional constraints: lengths, angles, radii.
- A fully defined sketch has no remaining degrees of freedom, so it cannot be dragged into a different shape by accident. Most packages show this with a colour change.
- Under-defined sketches change unpredictably when edited. Over-defined (conflicting) ones cause errors.

Common features
- Extrude: push a profile along a straight line, either to add material (boss) or to remove it (cut).
- Revolve: spin a profile about an axis. This is ideal for shafts, pulleys and other turned parts.
- Sweep: move a profile along a path, for example a bent tube.
- Loft: blend between two or more profiles.
- Fillet and chamfer: round or bevel edges.
- Shell: hollow out a solid to a uniform wall thickness.
- Hole wizard: standard drilled, counterbored and tapped holes.
- Patterns and mirrors: repeat features linearly, circularly or by symmetry.

The feature tree and design intent
Each feature depends on those before it (parent–child relationships). Design intent means building the model so that it changes in the way the design will need to:
- Dimension from functional datums, such as a bearing face, rather than from arbitrary edges.
- Use symmetry about the origin planes where the part is symmetric.
- Link related dimensions with equations or global variables, for example a bolt circle diameter.
- Add cosmetic features such as fillets late, so that deleting them does not break other features.
- Model the way the part will be made where that helps. A turned part is naturally a revolve; a milled plate is an extrude with pocket cuts.

Assemblies
Parts are combined with mates (constraints) that remove degrees of freedom.
- A free rigid body has 6 degrees of freedom: 3 translations and 3 rotations.
- A concentric mate between a pin and a hole removes 4, leaving 2: sliding along the axis and rotating about it.
- Adding a coincident mate between a shoulder and a face removes the sliding, leaving only rotation. This is how you model a working joint.
- Assemblies let you check interference and clearances, move mechanisms and produce a bill of materials.

Useful outputs
- Mass properties: mass, centre of mass, moments of inertia (these need the correct material assigned).
- 2D drawings that stay associated with the model (topic 6).
- Files for manufacture, such as STL for 3D printing or DXF profiles for laser cutting.

Exam tips: if asked how you would model a part, name the features in order, say which sketch plane and datums you would use, and explain how your choice captures design intent.

The design process takes a customer's need and turns it into a product that can be made, tested and used. Different textbooks draw it differently, for example Pahl and Beitz's phases or Pugh's "total design" model, but they share the same broad stages. The process is iterative: you often loop back when testing reveals a problem.

Stages
1. The brief. A short statement of the need, usually from a client, such as "a device to hold a phone at eye level on a desk". It is often vague or incomplete.
2. The product design specification (PDS). This turns the brief into clear requirements. Each requirement should be:
- Measurable, so you can test whether the design meets it ("supports a 250 g phone", not "strong").
- Solution-neutral: it says what is needed, not how to achieve it ("adjustable viewing angle between 30° and 70°", not "uses a hinge").
- Classified as a demand (must be met) or a wish (desirable). Pahl and Beitz use these terms.

Typical PDS headings include performance, environment, life, maintenance, target cost, quantity, size and weight, materials, manufacturing, standards and safety, ergonomics, aesthetics and disposal.
3. Concept generation. Produce many alternative solutions before judging any of them:
- Brainstorming and sketching.
- Function analysis: break the overall function into sub-functions such as "grip phone", "set angle" and "resist tipping".
- Morphological chart: list options for each sub-function, then combine one option from each row to form whole concepts.
4. Concept selection.
- Pugh's method: pick one concept as the datum. Score each other concept against it on each criterion as better (+), worse (−) or the same (S). Iterate, combining the strengths of good concepts.
- Weighted decision matrix: give each criterion a weight (summing to 1), score each concept (for example 1–5), and compare the weighted totals.
5. Embodiment design. Decide the layout, form, materials and main dimensions. Do the key calculations (strength, stiffness, stability).
6. Detail design. Fully define every part, with tolerances, materials and finishes, in drawings and a bill of materials.
7. Manufacture, testing and evaluation against the PDS. Every measurable requirement should be checked.

Worked example: weighted decision matrix
Weights: function 0.4, ease of manufacture 0.3, cost 0.2, appearance 0.1.

Scores out of 5 (function, manufacture, cost, appearance):
- Concept A: 4, 3, 2, 5 (unweighted total 14)
- Concept B: 3, 5, 4, 2 (unweighted total 14)
- Concept C: 5, 2, 3, 3 (unweighted total 13)

How the weighted totals are worked out:
- A = 0.4 × 4 + 0.3 × 3 + 0.2 × 2 + 0.1 × 5 = 3.4
- B = 0.4 × 3 + 0.3 × 5 + 0.2 × 4 + 0.1 × 2 = 3.7
- C = 0.4 × 5 + 0.3 × 2 + 0.2 × 3 + 0.1 × 3 = 3.5

B wins, even though A and B tie on unweighted totals (14 each). The weights matter, so they should be agreed and justified before scoring begins. A sensitivity check (do small changes to the weights change the winner?) shows how robust the choice is.

Records
Keep a design logbook: dated sketches, calculations, decisions and the reasons behind them. It shows how the design developed and is standard professional practice.

Exam tips: when asked for a PDS, write numbered requirements with values and units. When asked to select a concept, show the matrix and comment on how sensitive the result is.

Most machines take power from a motor and deliver it, at a different speed and torque, to where it is needed. This uses shafts, gears, belts or chains, bearings, and the means of locating and fixing them.

Power, torque and speed
- P = T ω, with ω = 2πN/60 (N in rpm, ω in rad/s).
- Example: a 2 kW motor at 1450 rpm. ω = 151.8 rad/s, so T = 2000/151.8 = 13.2 N m.
- Two common slips: dividing by rpm directly (giving 1.38 N m), or using rev/s instead of rad/s (giving 82.8 N m).

Gears
- Module: m = d/z, where d is the pitch circle diameter in mm and z is the number of teeth. Gears that mesh must have the same module and pressure angle (20° is standard).
- Gear ratio = z2/z1 = N1/N2.
- Ideal output torque = input torque × ratio. Real gears lose a little power, so multiply by the efficiency.
- Centre distance of an external pair: a = m(z1 + z2)/2.
- Example: m = 2 mm, z1 = 20, z2 = 60. Then d1 = 40 mm, d2 = 120 mm, the ratio is 3 and a = 80 mm.

Types of gear
- Spur gears: simple, with parallel shafts.
- Helical gears: quieter and stronger, but they produce an axial thrust.
- Bevel gears: shafts that intersect.
- Worm gears: high ratios in one stage, often hard or impossible to back-drive.

Belts and chains
- Belts and chains connect distant shafts.
- V-belts can slip, which protects against overload. Toothed (timing) belts and chains keep the speed ratio exact.

Shaft stresses (solid circular shaft of diameter d)
- Torsion: τ = T r / J with J = π d⁴/32, giving τ = 16T/(π d³).
- Bending: σ = M y / I with I = π d⁴/64, giving σ = 32M/(π d³).
- Combined bending and torsion, using the maximum shear stress (Tresca) criterion: τmax = 16√(M² + T²)/(π d³). Equivalently, use an equivalent torque Te = √(M² + T²).
- Example: T = 13.2 N m, M = 20 N m and allowable τ = 40 MPa give Te = 24.0 N m and d = (16 Te/(π τ))^(1/3) = 14.5 mm, so you would choose a standard size above this.
- With torsion only, d = 11.9 mm.

These are first-year static checks. A rotating shaft under bending sees fully reversed stress every revolution, so real designs also check fatigue, and the stress concentrations at shoulders and keyways matter a great deal.

Locating and fixing parts on shafts
- Axial location: shoulders, circlips (retaining rings), spacers, collars, locknuts.
- Torque transmission: keys in keyways, splines, interference fits, grub screws (light duty only).
- Bearings: deep groove ball bearings carry radial load plus some axial load. Normally one bearing is fixed axially and the other is allowed to float, so thermal expansion does not load the bearings.

Bearing life
The basic rating life, in millions of revolutions, is L10 = (C/P)^p, with p = 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. C is the dynamic load rating and P the equivalent load. 90% of a large group of identical bearings would be expected to reach this life.

Example: C = 14 kN and P = 2 kN give L10 = 7³ = 343 million revolutions. At 1450 rpm that is 343 × 10⁶/(1450 × 60) ≈ 3940 hours.

Exam tips: convert rpm to rad/s before using P = Tω, and keep N m, mm and MPa straight (1 MPa = 1 N/mm²). Check the gear module is the same on both gears.

A design is only good if it can be made at an acceptable cost and quality. Choosing a process depends on the material, the shape, the quantity, the tolerances and surface finish needed, and the cost.

Main process families
- Subtractive (machining): turning, milling, drilling, grinding. Accurate and flexible, good for one-offs and small batches, but it wastes material and takes time per part.
- Forming: bending sheet, forging, extrusion, rolling. Strong parts, little waste, but tooling is needed.
- Casting and moulding: sand casting (any quantity, rough finish), die casting (high volume, non-ferrous metals), injection moulding (high-volume plastics). Mould tooling is expensive, so these processes suit large quantities.
- Joining: welding, brazing and soldering, mechanical fasteners, adhesives.
- Cutting from sheet: laser cutting, waterjet cutting, punching.
- Additive manufacturing: fused deposition modelling (FDM, extruded thermoplastic), stereolithography (SLA, cured resin), selective laser sintering (SLS, powder). Excellent for prototypes and complex shapes, but slow per part and limited in material properties and accuracy.

Turning
The workpiece rotates in a lathe and a single-point tool removes material. Cutting speed is the surface speed of the work:
- V = π D N / 1000, with V in m/min, D in mm and N in rpm.
- So the spindle speed is N = 1000 V/(π D).
- Example: a 40 mm bar at a recommended cutting speed of 120 m/min needs N = 1000 × 120/(π × 40) = 955 rpm.
- Material removal rate is approximately V × f × ap, where f is the feed per revolution and ap the depth of cut. With V = 120 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev and ap = 2 mm, MRR = 120 000 × 0.2 × 2 = 48 000 mm³/min.

Milling
A rotating multi-tooth cutter removes material from work fed past it.
- Spindle speed: N = 1000 V/(π D), where D is the cutter diameter.
- Table feed rate: vf = fz × z × N, where fz is the feed per tooth and z the number of teeth.
- Example: a 4-flute, 10 mm cutter at V = 60 m/min and fz = 0.05 mm. N = 1910 rpm, vf = 0.05 × 4 × 1910 = 382 mm/min, and a 150 mm cut takes about 24 s, ignoring approach.

Drilling
Drilling uses the same speed formula with the drill diameter. Use standard drill sizes. For a metric coarse thread, the tapping drill is about the major diameter minus the pitch (8.5 mm for M10 × 1.5).

Design for manufacture (DfM)
- Internal corners of milled pockets have a radius at least equal to the cutter radius. Do not draw sharp internal corners.
- Avoid deep, narrow pockets and holes, because long tools deflect and chatter.
- Minimise the number of set-ups by keeping features accessible from as few directions as possible.
- Use standard hole sizes, threads and stock sizes.
- For moulded parts, keep the wall thickness uniform and add draft angles so parts release from the mould.
- Specify tight tolerances only where the function needs them, because cost rises steeply as tolerances tighten.

Workshop practice
Safety comes first: safety glasses, no loose clothing or jewellery, guards in place, and swarf removed with a brush, never by hand. Before cutting, plan the order of operations (a process plan): which face to machine first so it can serve as a datum, how to hold the work, and which tools and speeds to use.

Exam tips: always state the units in speed calculations, and justify your process choice using quantity, material, geometry and tolerance.

Although the 3D model defines the geometry, the 2D drawing is still the usual contract document for manufacture and inspection. It carries the dimensions, tolerances, materials, finishes and notes that the workshop needs. In the UK, drawings follow BS 8888 (Technical product documentation and specification), which brings together the relevant ISO standards.

Views
- Drawing views are generated from the model and remain associated with it, so a change to the model updates the drawing.
- Choose the front view to show the most characteristic shape, then add only the views needed to define the part fully.
- Use section views to show internal features, detail views (enlarged) for small features, and auxiliary views for inclined faces.
- Show the projection symbol and keep the views aligned.

Dimensioning principles
- Dimension each feature once only, in the view where it is clearest. Do not repeat dimensions in other views.
- Dimension from functional datums, the faces or axes that locate the part in its assembly.
- Avoid long chains of dimensions where tolerances would accumulate. Prefer parallel dimensioning from a common datum when position matters.
- Do not dimension to hidden lines. Use a section instead.
- Place dimensions outside the outline where possible, and keep them clear of each other.
- Use the symbols Ø (diameter) and R (radius). State linear dimensions in millimetres, with the unit given once in the title block.

Features with their own notation
- Holes: diameter, depth, and counterbore or countersink details. For example, "Ø6.6 THRU" or "4× Ø6.6 equally spaced on Ø50 PCD".
- Threads: "M10" means an ISO metric coarse thread with a 10 mm nominal (major) diameter and a 1.5 mm pitch. A fine thread states its pitch, such as M10 × 1.25. Threads are drawn conventionally rather than with every turn shown.
- Chamfers (for example 1 × 45°), fillets, surface texture symbols and geometric tolerances (topic 7).

Title block
A typical title block contains:
- The drawing title and drawing number
- The scale
- The projection symbol
- The units
- The material and finish
- The general tolerances (for example by reference to ISO 2768)
- The author, checker and date
- The revision and the sheet number

Many drawings also state that they are drawn to BS 8888.

Assembly drawings
- Show how the parts fit together, usually with sections.
- Each part is identified by a numbered balloon that refers to a parts list (bill of materials). The list gives the item number, part name, drawing number, material and quantity.
- Overall and interface dimensions only. The detail drawings carry the full part dimensions.

Checking a drawing
Before releasing a drawing, check it:
- Could someone make the part from this drawing alone?
- Is any feature unlocated or undimensioned?
- Are any dimensions duplicated?
- Are the tolerances achievable by the process you intend to use?

Exam tips: you will rarely be asked to reproduce the standard. You will be asked to spot errors (missing centre lines, duplicate or chained dimensions, dimensions to hidden lines, a missing projection symbol) and to explain how to fix them.

notes.h: Variation, limits and fits, and tolerances
notes.body:
No manufacturing process makes two parts exactly alike. Tolerancing states how much variation is acceptable so that parts still fit and work, and so that parts made in different places are interchangeable.

Basic terms
- Nominal size: the size used to name the feature, for example Ø25.
- Limits: the largest and smallest permitted sizes.
- Tolerance: the difference between the limits.
- Deviations: the limits measured from the nominal size, such as +0.021/0.

ISO system of limits and fits (ISO 286)
- Each toleranced size is written as a letter and a number, such as H7 or g6.
- The number is the international tolerance (IT) grade: a bigger number means a wider tolerance. For sizes from 18 to 30 mm, IT6 = 13 µm and IT7 = 21 µm.
- The letter is the fundamental deviation, which sets where the tolerance zone sits relative to the nominal size. Capital letters are for holes and lower case for shafts.
- H holes have a lower deviation of zero, and h shafts have an upper deviation of zero.
- The hole-basis system, with the hole at H and the fit chosen by the shaft letter, is usual, because standard reamers and gauges make holes and shafts are easier to vary.

Examples for Ø25 with an H7 hole (25.000 to 25.021 mm)
- H7/g6, sliding fit. The shaft is 24.980 to 24.993 mm, giving a clearance of 0.007 to 0.041 mm.
- H7/h6, locational clearance fit. The shaft is 24.987 to 25.000 mm, giving a clearance of 0 to 0.034 mm.
- H7/k6, transition fit. The shaft is 25.002 to 25.015 mm, so the result ranges from 0.019 mm clearance to 0.015 mm interference.
- H7/p6, locational interference fit. The shaft is 25.022 to 25.035 mm, giving an interference of 0.001 to 0.035 mm. Assembly needs a press, or heating of the hub.

How the fit limits are found:
- Maximum clearance = largest hole − smallest shaft.
- Minimum clearance = smallest hole − largest shaft. A negative value means interference.

General tolerances
Dimensions without their own tolerance take a general tolerance. ISO 2768-1 has classes f (fine), m (medium), c (coarse) and v (very coarse). For class m, a dimension over 6 mm and up to 30 mm is ±0.2 mm, and one over 30 mm and up to 120 mm is ±0.3 mm.

Geometric tolerances (ISO 1101)
Size tolerances alone do not control shape or position, so geometric tolerances are added, referred to datums where needed:
- Form: flatness, straightness, circularity, cylindricity.
- Orientation: parallelism, perpendicularity, angularity.
- Location: position, concentricity, symmetry.
- Run-out: circular run-out, total run-out.

Each is shown in a feature control frame: the symbol, the tolerance value and the datum letters.

Tolerance stack-up
When several parts add up in a chain, their variations combine.
- Worst case: the tolerances add. Three parts at ±0.1, ±0.05 and ±0.05 give ±0.20 mm.
- Statistical (root sum of squares, RSS): √(0.1² + 0.05² + 0.05²) = ±0.12 mm. This assumes independent, centred, normally distributed variation, and is far more economical for long stacks.

Process capability
A process with standard deviation σ and mean μ, set against specification limits USL and LSL:
- Cp = (USL − LSL)/(6σ) measures potential capability.
- Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/(3σ) also accounts for the process being off-centre.
- Example: limits 9.95–10.05 mm, μ = 10.01 mm, σ = 0.012 mm. Cp = 1.39 and Cpk = 1.11, so recentring the process would help.

Exam tips: show the hole and shaft limits explicitly before working out the clearance, and say whether a fit is clearance, transition or interference.

cards.b: Mould tooling is very expensive but each part takes seconds and needs little finishing, so cost per part falls sharply with quantity.
A milled pocket's internal corners can be no sharper than the cutter radius, so drawings should specify a suitable radius.

cards.b: Approximately major diameter minus pitch, e.g. 8.5 mm for M10 × 1.5.
UK standard for technical product documentation and specification; it draws together the ISO standards for engineering drawings and tolerancing.

cards.f: Why dimension from a datum, not in a chain
cards.b: In a chain each tolerance adds to the next, so the position of the last feature varies widely. Dimensions from a common datum keep each feature's tolerance independent.
Title, drawing number, scale, projection symbol, units, material and finish, general tolerances, author, checker, date, revision, sheet number.
On an assembly drawing, numbered balloons identify each part and refer to the parts list (item, name, drawing number, material, quantity).
An enlarged view of a small area of a drawing, labelled and scaled, used to dimension small features clearly.
The hole is made to an H tolerance (lower deviation zero) and the shaft tolerance is chosen to give the required fit.
International tolerance grade: the number in a fit designation (e.g. 7 in H7). A larger number means a wider tolerance; for 18–30 mm, IT7 = 21 µm.
Clearance: always a gap. Interference: shaft always larger than hole. Transition: may give either, depending on actual sizes.
Hole 25.000–25.021, shaft 24.980–24.993: clearance 0.007–0.041 mm (sliding fit).
Worst case adds the tolerances (Σti). RSS takes √(Σti²), assuming independent, centred, normal variation, so it gives a smaller predicted spread.
Cp = (USL − LSL)/6σ (potential capability); Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/3σ (accounts for off-centre mean).
Medium class: ±0.2 mm for dimensions over 6 up to 30 mm; ±0.3 mm over 30 up to 120 mm.
Form (flatness, straightness, circularity, cylindricity), orientation, location (position), and run-out, shown in a feature control frame.

questions.q: In a first-angle orthographic drawing, where is the plan (the view from above) placed?
options: To the right of the front view
questions.why: In first-angle projection the object sits between the viewer and the plane, so the view from above is projected onto the plane beneath the object and drawn below the front view. Placing the plan above the front view is the third-angle convention. The position to the right of the front view holds the view from the left in first angle. Views are not placed freely: their positions follow from the projection method shown by the symbol.

questions.q: Which line type is used for hidden edges on an engineering drawing?
questions.why: Hidden edges use a dashed narrow line. The long-dash dotted narrow line marks centre lines and axes of symmetry. Continuous narrow lines are for dimensions, projection lines, leaders and hatching. Continuous wide lines show visible outlines.

questions.q: Explain the difference between first-angle and third-angle projection, and how a reader can tell which one a drawing uses.
markScheme: First angle: object between viewer and plane; plan below the front view, view from the left placed on the right
Third angle: plane between viewer and object; plan above the front view, view from the left placed on the left
The projection symbol (truncated cone) in the title block shows which is used
The symbol is read as a small drawing: first angle places the end view (circles) opposite the end it views; third angle places it on the same side
questions.modelAnswer: Both methods show the object in a set of orthographic views, but they arrange them differently. In first-angle projection, the object is imagined between the viewer and the projection plane. So the view from above (plan) is drawn below the front view, and the view from the left is drawn to the right of it. In third-angle projection, the plane is between the viewer and the object. So the plan is drawn above the front view, and the view from the left is drawn on the left. A reader tells them apart from the projection symbol, a truncated cone shown in side and end view. The symbol is itself a small first- or third-angle drawing: in first angle the end view sits on the opposite side from the end it views, in third angle on the same side. Every drawing should show the symbol, because reading a drawing in the wrong projection mirrors the part.

questions.q: In a CAD assembly, a cylindrical pin is given a single concentric mate with a hole in a fixed plate. How many degrees of freedom does the pin have left?
questions.why: A free body has 6 degrees of freedom. A concentric mate fixes the pin's axis to the hole's axis, which removes two translations and two rotations perpendicular to the axis. Sliding along the axis and rotating about it remain, so 2 are left. Four left would mean the mate removed only the two perpendicular translations. One left would need a further mate, such as a shoulder against the plate, to stop the sliding. Zero would mean the pin was fully fixed, which a single concentric mate cannot achieve.

questions.q: Which modelling choice best captures design intent for a symmetric bracket?
options: Add all fillets first so the shape looks finished early
Leave sketches under-defined so they are easier to drag later
Sketch the profile symmetric about the origin plane and dimension holes from functional datums
Draw the profile anywhere and position each hole from the nearest edge
questions.why: Symmetry about an origin plane and dimensions taken from functional datums mean the model updates correctly when sizes change. Positioning holes from whichever edge is nearest ties them to features that may move, so edits can shift the holes unpredictably. Adding fillets early creates many parent–child links that break when the base geometry changes, so fillets are usually added last. Under-defined sketches can change shape by accident, which works against design intent.

questions.q: Describe how you would model a stepped shaft with a keyway and a chamfer at each end in a parametric CAD package, explaining how your approach captures design intent.
markScheme: Sketch half the longitudinal profile on a plane through the axis, with the centre line on the origin; fully define it
Revolve the profile about the axis to form the stepped shaft
Dimension step lengths from the functional datum (e.g. bearing shoulder) and diameters directly; link related values if needed
Add the keyway as an extruded cut from a sketch on a tangent plane, positioned from the relevant shoulder
Add chamfers last; use standard values; this keeps the parent–child structure robust
questions.modelAnswer: I would sketch half the shaft profile (the outline of the steps) on a plane containing the axis. The axis would be a centre line through the origin, and I would fully define the sketch with diameters and step lengths. Lengths would be dimensioned from the functional datum, such as the bearing shoulder, so that the important fits keep their positions when other lengths change. I would then revolve the profile through 360° to form the solid, which mirrors the way the shaft would be turned on a lathe. For the keyway, I would create a plane tangent to the relevant diameter, sketch the keyway outline located from the shoulder that positions the hub, and use an extruded cut to the key depth. The chamfers would be added last as separate features, so they can be changed or removed without breaking the earlier features. Building it this way keeps the feature tree simple and makes the important dimensions easy to edit.

questions.q: Weights: function 0.4, manufacture 0.3, cost 0.2, appearance 0.1. Scores (out of 5) — A: 4, 3, 2, 5; B: 3, 5, 4, 2; C: 5, 2, 3, 3. Which concept has the highest weighted score?
questions.why: Weighted totals are A = 1.6 + 0.9 + 0.4 + 0.5 = 3.4, B = 1.2 + 1.5 + 0.8 + 0.2 = 3.7 and C = 2.0 + 0.6 + 0.6 + 0.3 = 3.5, so B is highest. A's 3.4 is correct for A, but it is the lowest of the three. C's 3.5 is correct for C, but C is still behind B. The tie on 14 comes from adding the raw scores and ignoring the weights.

questions.q: Which is the best-written requirement for the PDS of an electric kettle?
options: Boils 1.0 L of water from 15 °C in under 3 minutes
questions.why: A good requirement is measurable and solution-neutral, and boiling a stated volume from a stated temperature within a time limit can be tested directly. 'Quickly' cannot be tested because it gives no value. Specifying a 3 kW concealed element prescribes the solution rather than the need. 'Modern and attractive' is subjective, with no test or criterion.

questions.q: Explain how Pugh's concept selection method works and why it is useful early in a design project.
markScheme: Choose a datum concept (often an existing product or one promising concept)
Compare each concept with the datum on each criterion from the PDS: better (+), worse (−) or same (S)
Sum the pluses and minuses, but use them to guide discussion rather than as a precise score
Combine the strengths of good concepts, drop weak ones, change the datum and repeat (controlled convergence)
Useful early because it needs only relative judgements, not detailed data, and encourages new hybrid concepts
questions.modelAnswer: In Pugh's method, the criteria come from the PDS and the concepts are listed as columns of a matrix. One concept, or an existing product, is chosen as the datum. Each other concept is compared with it on each criterion and marked better (+), worse (−) or the same (S). The numbers of pluses and minuses are counted. They are not treated as a precise score, but they show where each concept is strong or weak. The team then improves weak concepts by borrowing strengths from others, drops concepts that are clearly worse, picks a new datum (often the strongest concept) and repeats the comparison. Pugh called this controlled convergence. The method suits early design because it needs only relative judgements, not detailed calculations or costs. It also tends to generate improved hybrid concepts rather than just picking a winner.

questions.q: Two external spur gears of module 2 mm have 20 and 60 teeth. What is their centre distance?
questions.why: a = m(z1 + z2)/2 = 2 × 80/2 = 80 mm, half the sum of the pitch diameters (40 mm and 120 mm). 160 mm adds the two diameters without halving them. 40 mm uses m(z2 − z1)/2, which is the formula for an internal (annulus) gear pair, not two external gears. 120 mm is just the pitch diameter of the larger gear.

questions.q: A motor delivers 2 kW at 1450 rpm. What is the torque on its shaft?
questions.why: T = P/ω = 2000/(2π × 1450/60) = 2000/151.8 = 13.2 N m. 1.38 N m divides the power by the rpm directly. 82.8 N m converts rpm to revolutions per second but leaves out the 2π needed for rad/s. 0.0132 N m leaves the power in kW instead of converting it to W.

questions.q: A solid steel shaft transmits a torque of 13.2 N m and carries a bending moment of 20 N m. Using the maximum shear stress criterion with an allowable shear stress of 40 MPa, find the minimum diameter, and state two further things a real design must consider.
markScheme: d = 14.5 mm, so choose the next standard size up (e.g. 15 or 16 mm)

Further considerations (any two): fatigue from reversed bending in a rotating shaft; stress concentrations at shoulders, keyways and circlip grooves; deflection and stiffness at bearings and gears; critical speed
questions.modelAnswer: Under the maximum shear stress criterion, the equivalent torque is Te = √(M² + T²) = √(400 + 174) = 24.0 N m. Setting τ = 16Te/(π d³) = 40 × 10⁶ Pa gives d³ = 16 × 24.0/(π × 40 × 10⁶) = 3.05 × 10⁻⁶ m³, so d = 0.0145 m = 14.5 mm. A standard size above this, such as 15 or 16 mm, would be chosen. A real design must also consider fatigue: in a rotating shaft the bending stress reverses every revolution. It must also allow for stress concentrations at shoulders, keyways and circlip grooves, which raise the local stress. Shaft deflection matters too, because too much slope or deflection at bearings and gears causes poor meshing and early wear.

questions.q: A 40 mm diameter bar is to be turned at a cutting speed of 120 m/min. What spindle speed is needed?
questions.why: N = 1000V/(πD) = 1000 × 120/(π × 40) = 955 rpm. 3000 rpm leaves π out of the formula. 1910 rpm uses the 20 mm radius in place of the diameter. 0.95 rpm leaves out the factor of 1000 that converts metres to millimetres.

questions.q: Which process is most suitable for making 100 000 identical small ABS plastic housings?
questions.why: Injection moulding has high tooling cost but very low cost per part and short cycle times, so it suits large runs of plastic parts. CNC milling each housing from solid would be slow and wasteful at this volume. FDM is far too slow per part and gives a poorer finish, which suits prototypes. Sand casting is used for metals, not ABS, and gives a rough finish.

questions.q: A slot 150 mm long is to be milled with a 10 mm, 4-flute cutter. The recommended cutting speed is 60 m/min and the feed per tooth is 0.05 mm. Find the spindle speed, the table feed rate and the cutting time. Give one design-for-manufacture point about the slot.
markScheme: t = 150/382 = 0.39 min ≈ 24 s (ignoring approach and overrun)
DfM point, e.g. slot ends will have a 5 mm radius (cutter radius), so do not specify square ends; use a standard cutter width; avoid excessive depth-to-width ratio
questions.modelAnswer: Spindle speed N = 1000 × 60/(π × 10) = 1910 rpm. Table feed vf = fz × z × N = 0.05 × 4 × 1910 = 382 mm/min. Cutting time = 150/382 = 0.39 min, about 24 s, plus a little extra for the cutter to approach and clear the work. A design-for-manufacture point: the ends of a slot cut with a 10 mm end mill are semicircular with a 5 mm radius, so the drawing should allow this rather than demand square ends, which would need extra operations. Making the slot width equal to a standard cutter size also avoids a second pass.

questions.q: What does the thread callout 'M10' mean on a metric drawing?
options: ISO metric coarse thread, 10 mm major diameter, 1.5 mm pitch
A thread with 10 threads per inch
A thread with a 10 mm minor (root) diameter
A thread with a 10 mm pitch
questions.why: M denotes an ISO metric thread and the number is the nominal major diameter in mm. With no pitch stated, it is the coarse series, which is 1.5 mm for M10. Threads per inch belong to imperial systems such as UNC, not metric callouts. The minor (root) diameter of M10 is only about 8.2–8.4 mm, so 10 mm is not the minor diameter. A 10 mm pitch would be far too coarse for a 10 mm thread, and pitch is written after the size, as in M10 × 1.25.

questions.q: Which of these is good dimensioning practice?
options: Chain-dimensioning a row of holes from one to the next
Dimensioning each feature once, from a functional datum
Dimensioning to hidden lines to avoid adding a section view
Repeating key dimensions in every view for clarity
questions.why: Each feature should be dimensioned once, from the datum that matters for its function. Dimensioning to hidden lines is ambiguous, and a section should be used instead. Repeating dimensions creates the risk of conflicting values when one is changed. Chain dimensioning makes tolerances accumulate along the row, so the last hole's position varies much more than the first's.

questions.q: List the information you would expect in the title block of a detail drawing produced to BS 8888, and explain why the general tolerance note matters.
markScheme: Title and drawing number; scale; projection symbol; units
Material and finish
Author, checker, date, revision, sheet number
General tolerance note (e.g. ISO 2768-m) gives the permitted variation for every dimension without its own tolerance, so all dimensions have defined limits
questions.modelAnswer: The title block should give the part title and a unique drawing number, the scale, the projection symbol and the units (normally millimetres). It should also state the material and any finish or treatment, the names of the author and checker, the date, the revision letter or number, and the sheet number. The general tolerance note, for example a reference to ISO 2768 class m, matters because no real part can be made exactly to size. Every dimension needs limits. The note sets the limits for all dimensions that do not carry their own tolerance, so the workshop knows how accurate to be, and the inspector knows what to accept, without every dimension being toleranced individually.

questions.q: For a Ø25 H7/g6 fit (H7: 0/+0.021 mm; g6: −0.020/−0.007 mm), what is the range of clearance?
questions.why: Minimum clearance = smallest hole − largest shaft = 25.000 − 24.993 = 0.007 mm. Maximum clearance = largest hole − smallest shaft = 25.021 − 24.980 = 0.041 mm. The range 0 to 0.034 mm belongs to H7/h6, where the shaft's upper deviation is zero. The transition range (0.015 mm interference to 0.019 mm clearance) belongs to H7/k6. The interference range 0.001 to 0.035 mm belongs to H7/p6.

questions.q: Three parts stacked end to end have tolerances of ±0.10, ±0.05 and ±0.05 mm. What are the worst-case and root-sum-square (RSS) tolerances on the total length?
questions.why: Worst case adds the tolerances: 0.10 + 0.05 + 0.05 = ±0.20 mm. RSS gives √(0.10² + 0.05² + 0.05²) = √0.015 = ±0.12 mm. Giving ±0.20 mm for both ignores the fact that RSS assumes the deviations rarely all reach their limits together. Giving ±0.12 mm worst case and ±0.20 mm RSS swaps the two results; RSS can never exceed worst case. ±0.067 mm is just the mean of the three tolerances, which has no meaning for a stack.

questions.q: A turned diameter is specified as 10.00 ± 0.05 mm. Measurements show a process mean of 10.01 mm and a standard deviation of 0.012 mm. Calculate Cp and Cpk and interpret the results.
markScheme: Interpretation: the spread fits in the tolerance (Cp > 1.33 often taken as capable), but the mean is off-centre so Cpk is lower; recentring to 10.00 would raise Cpk towards 1.39
questions.modelAnswer: The limits are USL = 10.05 mm and LSL = 9.95 mm. Cp = (USL − LSL)/(6σ) = 0.10/(6 × 0.012) = 0.10/0.072 = 1.39. Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/(3σ) = min(0.04, 0.06)/0.036 = 0.04/0.036 = 1.11. A Cp of 1.39 shows the natural spread of the process (6σ = 0.072 mm) fits comfortably within the 0.10 mm tolerance. The lower Cpk shows the mean is shifted 0.01 mm towards the upper limit, so oversize parts are more likely than undersize ones. Many companies use 1.33 as a minimum target. Recentring the process on 10.00 mm would bring Cpk up to equal Cp, at 1.39.

questions.q: A 2.0 kW electric motor running at 1450 rpm drives a machine through a single-stage spur gear pair. The pinion has 20 teeth and the wheel 60 teeth, module 2 mm; the gear efficiency is 97%. (a) Find the pinion torque, the output speed and the output torque. [5] (b) Find the pitch diameters and the centre distance. [3] (c) Size the output shaft for torsion only, with an allowable shear stress of 40 MPa, and choose a sensible diameter. [4] (d) The output shaft runs in deep groove ball bearings with C = 14 kN, each carrying an equivalent load of 2 kN. Estimate the L10 life in hours. [4] (e) Suggest how the wheel should be fixed to the output shaft axially and for torque, and a suitable ISO fit for the wheel bore. [4]
markScheme: (c) d = (16T/(πτ))^(1/3) = (16 × 38.3/(π × 40 × 10⁶))^(1/3) = 17.0 mm; choose e.g. 20 mm to allow for the keyway, stress concentrations and bending
(e) Axial: shoulder on one side plus circlip, spacer or collar on the other; torque: parallel key in keyway (or spline)
(e) Fit: e.g. H7/k6 transition (or H7/h6 locational clearance with key carrying torque) for accurate location that can still be assembled; justify
Correct units and clear working throughout
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Pinion speed ω1 = 2π × 1450/60 = 151.8 rad/s, so the pinion torque T1 = 2000/151.8 = 13.2 N m. The ratio is 60/20 = 3, so the output speed is 1450/3 = 483 rpm. The output torque allows for the efficiency: T2 = 13.2 × 3 × 0.97 = 38.3 N m. Check: P2 = T2 ω2 = 38.3 × 2π × 483.3/60 = 1940 W = 0.97 × 2000 W.

(b) Pitch diameters: d1 = m z1 = 2 × 20 = 40 mm and d2 = 2 × 60 = 120 mm. Centre distance a = m(z1 + z2)/2 = 2 × 80/2 = 80 mm.

(c) For torsion only, τ = 16T/(πd³), so d = (16 × 38.3/(π × 40 × 10⁶))^(1/3) = (4.88 × 10⁻⁶)^(1/3) m = 17.0 mm. This ignores the bending from the gear tooth load, the keyway and the stress concentrations at shoulders, as well as fatigue, so a larger standard size such as 20 mm would be chosen. At 20 mm the torsional stress is 16 × 38.3/(π × 0.02³) = 24.4 MPa, which leaves margin for those effects.

(d) For ball bearings, L10 = (C/P)³ = (14/2)³ = 343 million revolutions. At 483.3 rpm that is 343 × 10⁶/(483.3 × 60) = 11 800 hours, roughly 1.3 years of continuous running. Ninety per cent of such bearings would be expected to reach it.

(e) Axially, the wheel would be located against a shoulder on the shaft on one side and held by a circlip, spacer or collar on the other. Torque would be carried by a parallel key in keyways in the shaft and the hub (or by a spline for higher torque). The bore needs accurate location so the gear runs true, but must still be assembled in the workshop. A transition fit such as H7/k6 (for Ø20, roughly 0.019 mm clearance to 0.015 mm interference) is a common choice, with the key transmitting the torque. A locational clearance fit H7/h6 is acceptable if easy assembly matters more. A heavy interference fit is unnecessary when a key is used.

questions.q: You are asked to design and make, in a university workshop, a desk stand that holds a smartphone at a comfortable viewing angle. Describe how you would take this project from brief to finished part. Include an example PDS (at least six measurable requirements), how you would generate and select concepts, how you would use CAD and drawings, and how you would plan manufacture and tolerancing.
markScheme: Brief clarified with the client/user; PDS with at least six measurable, solution-neutral requirements (e.g. phone sizes, angle range, stability, mass, cost, manufacturing constraints)
Concept generation: function analysis (hold phone, set angle, resist tipping, allow charging), sketching, morphological chart; several distinct concepts
Concept selection with Pugh matrix and/or weighted matrix; criteria from PDS; sensitivity of result
Embodiment: material and process choice (e.g. laser-cut acrylic, milled aluminium, FDM) justified by workshop capability; key calculations (tipping stability)
CAD: fully defined sketches, design intent, assembly with mates to check fit and range of movement; drawings to BS 8888 with title block and projection symbol
Tolerancing: general tolerances (ISO 2768-m) plus specific fits where parts interact (e.g. pivot pin H7/g6 clearance or similar)
Manufacture plan: operations sequence, datums, fixturing, speeds; safety; logbook records
Testing against each PDS requirement and iteration
questions.modelAnswer:
Brief and PDS. I would first clarify the brief with the user: which phones, used for what (video calls, reading), and on what kind of desk. Then I would write a PDS with measurable, solution-neutral requirements, for example: (1) holds phones 65–80 mm wide and 7–12 mm thick, including in a case; (2) viewing angle adjustable between 50° and 80° from horizontal; (3) does not tip over when the screen is tapped with a 5 N horizontal force at the top of the phone; (4) allows a charging cable to be plugged in while the phone is in place; (5) mass under 400 g and footprint within 100 × 120 mm; (6) material cost under £10; (7) can be made with the department's workshop processes in under 3 hours; (8) no sharp edges. I would label each requirement a demand or a wish.

Concepts. Function analysis splits the task into: support the phone, set the angle, resist tipping and route the cable. I would sketch several options for each and combine them in a morphological chart, for example a folded sheet, a slotted base with a tilting cradle, or a two-piece interlocking plate design. This would give four or five distinct concepts.

Selection. I would use a Pugh matrix against the PDS criteria, with a simple concept as the datum, and improve the best concepts by combining strengths. A weighted decision matrix would confirm the choice, with a check on whether small changes to the weights change the winner.

Embodiment and CAD. Suppose I chose a two-plate design in aluminium, milled and drilled, with a pivot pin and a friction knob. I would check tipping stability by taking moments about the front edge of the base: the stand's weight must provide a larger restoring moment than the 5 N tap. I would model each part with fully defined sketches dimensioned from functional datums, build an assembly with mates to check the range of angles and clearances, and run interference checks. I would then produce detail drawings to BS 8888, each with views, sections where needed, a title block, the projection symbol and the material.

Tolerancing. Most dimensions can take a general tolerance such as ISO 2768-m. The pivot needs a deliberate fit, such as an H7 hole with a g6 pin (a sliding clearance fit), so the angle can be adjusted but the joint does not wobble. Slot widths that receive the other plate would also be toleranced so the plates assemble.

Manufacture and test. I would write a process plan: cut the stock, face a datum edge, mill the profiles and slots, drill and ream the pivot hole, deburr, then assemble. For each operation I would note the work-holding, the tools and the speeds (N = 1000V/(πD)), and follow workshop safety rules. I would record everything in a logbook. Finally, I would test the stand against each PDS requirement, including phone sizes, angle range, tipping force and cable access, and iterate on anything it fails.
